how_to_obtain: Code review for the canonical library-misuse pattern: grep the verifier configuration for any allow-list that includes 'none' or that is absent entirely (no algorithms parameter). RFC 8725 §3.1 'Perform Algorithm Verification' + §3.2 'Use Appropriate Algorithms' require an explicit allow-list excluding 'none'.

Library API check — confirm the verifier is invoked with an explicit algorithms parameter: node-jsonwebtoken `jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['RS256'] })`; jjwt `Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(key).build()` (rejects alg=none by default since 0.10.x); PyJWT `jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256'])`. Calls without an algorithms parameter historically accept alg=none.

Live probe: craft a test JWT with header `{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}`, payload of choice, empty signature segment, present it to the protected endpoint. Per OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet (alg=none section) the verifier MUST return 401; a 200 confirms accepts_alg_none=true. Fires exposure "JWT signature algorithm confusion".

CVE precedent: cross-check the library version against CVE-2015-9235 (node-jsonwebtoken alg=none) and CVE-2018-1000531 (inversoft prime-jwt) — older pinned versions remain vulnerable even when the current API is safe.

Authorization server config: inspect the token-service configuration for the access-token TTL setting (Keycloak realm 'Access Token Lifespan'; Auth0 API 'Token Expiration'; Okta authorization-server policy 'Access Token Lifetime'; Cognito user-pool client 'AccessTokenValidity').

Decode an issued token: `echo <jwt> | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | jq '.exp - .iat'` returns the lifetime in seconds; divide by 60. The exp/iat pair is the authoritative on-wire value regardless of stated config.

RFC 9700 §2.2 baseline: 'Authorization servers SHOULD use short-lived access tokens.' OWASP OAuth2 Cheat Sheet — 'Token Lifetime' recommends minutes-scale (typical 5–15 min). Rule "Excessive token lifetime with no revocation channel" fires at > 60 min.
Confirm there is no silent renewal extending an apparent short TTL: check whether the resource server re-stamps tokens server-side or whether refresh is the only renewal channel.

option_name: Audience (aud) claim enforced against this service
how_to_obtain: Verifier configuration: confirm the expected aud value is configured and enforced. node-jsonwebtoken `jwt.verify(token, key, { audience: 'api.example.com' })`; PyJWT `jwt.decode(token, key, audience='api.example.com')`; jjwt `.requireAudience('api.example.com')` on the parser builder. Absence of these calls means aud is decoded but not enforced.
RFC 8725 §3.7 'Use and Validate Audience' + RFC 7519 §4.1.3: verifier MUST reject tokens whose aud does not name this service.

Live probe: take a valid token minted by the same issuer for a different audience (a sibling service that shares signing keys) and present it here. A 200 response proves audience_claim_validated=false — the audience-confusion replay path fires exposure "Missing or permissive token claim validation".
Log review: confirm verification-failure logs distinguish 'audience mismatch' from 'signature invalid' — presence of the former in deny logs is positive evidence the check runs.

Capture Set-Cookie on login: `curl -i -X POST https://app.example.com/login -d 'user=...&pass=...' | grep -i '^set-cookie:'` and verify each session cookie line contains `HttpOnly` (case-insensitive).
Browser DevTools: Application → Cookies pane — the HttpOnly column must be checked for the session cookie.

OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — 'Cookies' section: HttpOnly is mandatory; without it `document.cookie` from injected script reads the token. Missing HttpOnly fires exposure "Token exfiltration via XSS / JS-accessible storage".
Live browser-console test: `document.cookie` must NOT return the session id. If it does, HttpOnly is absent (or set on a different cookie than the session-bearing one).

Verifier code path: confirm the library's default exp/nbf check is not disabled — node-jsonwebtoken default validates exp (disabled only by `ignoreExpiration: true`); PyJWT default validates exp (`options={'verify_exp': False}` disables it); jjwt validates exp by default through the parser.
RFC 7519 §4.1.4 (exp) + §4.1.5 (nbf) + RFC 8725 §3.8: tokens past exp or before nbf MUST be rejected.

Live probe: present a token whose exp is in the past (decode an old one or mint a test token with `exp: now-3600`). A 200 proves expiry is not enforced; a 401 with 'token expired' confirms the check. Missing expiry validation fires exposure "Missing or permissive token claim validation".
Inspect any clock-skew tolerance — RFC 7519 allows 'small leeway' (~60s typical, e.g. PyJWT `leeway=60`); leeway beyond a few minutes weakens but does not disable the control.

Operator interview / secret-management inspection: locate the HS256/HS384/HS512 shared secret in the secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, env var) and measure its byte length: entropy_bits = 8 × len(secret) for CSPRNG-generated random bytes, or much lower for human-chosen strings.

RFC 7518 §3.2 'HMAC with SHA-2 Functions': 'A key of the same size as the hash output (for instance, 256 bits for HS256) or larger MUST be used.' Floor is 256 bits per RFC; rule "Weak HMAC secret brute-force" fires below 128 bits.
Offline attempt as proof: capture a JWT and run `hashcat -m 16500 token.txt rockyou.txt` (or `jwt2john` → john) — a hit within minutes proves entropy is well below the floor.

If the secret is passphrase-derived, require the KDF to be Argon2/PBKDF2 with documented work factor (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet); otherwise treat the passphrase's own entropy as the bit count.

Verifier configuration: confirm an explicit issuer is configured — node-jsonwebtoken `{ issuer: 'https://idp.example.com' }`; PyJWT `issuer='https://idp.example.com'`; jjwt `.requireIssuer(...)` on the parser builder.
RFC 7519 §4.1.1 (iss) + RFC 8725 §3.7 ('Use and Validate Issuer'): verifier MUST match iss against a trusted issuer list, rejecting tokens minted by any other authority.

Live probe: mint or capture a token from a different issuer signed with a key the verifier trusts (e.g. a sibling tenant on the same authorization server) and present it. Acceptance proves iss is not enforced — fires exposure "Missing or permissive token claim validation".
Cross-tenant test: if the deployment is multi-tenant, present tenant-A's token at tenant-B's endpoint — a 200 indicates issuer scoping is missing.

Code grep for the library-misuse pattern: search for `jwt.decode(` (node-jsonwebtoken — decode-without-verify), `jwt.get_unverified_claims(` (PyJWT / python-jose), `Jwts.parser().parse(` without `.setSigningKey()`, or any 'unverified' / 'insecure' helper.
RFC 8725 §2.1 'Perform Algorithm Verification' + OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet — 'Use a Proper JWT Library': the verify path must include signature verification, not solely claim decoding.

Live probe: tamper a single byte of an issued JWT payload (re-base64-encode payload with a changed claim, keep original signature) and present it. The verifier MUST return 401 — a 200 conclusively proves jwt_signature_verified=false. Fires exposure "JWT signature algorithm confusion".
Audit-log review: signature failures should produce a distinct error code from 'expired' or 'audience mismatch' — absence of any 'signature invalid' deny events over a sample period is suspicious.

option_name: Multi-day token persisted in browser-side storage
how_to_obtain: Browser DevTools: Application → Local Storage / Session Storage — enumerate stored keys; any value that decodes as a JWT with `exp - iat > 86400`, or any opaque token labelled `refresh_token`, is a long-lived browser-stored credential.

RFC 9700 §4.13 'Browser-Based Apps': refresh tokens stored in browser storage are a primary XSS exfiltration target; the BCP recommends server-side session backends or HttpOnly cookies for long-lived material.

OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet — 'Token Storage on Client Side': localStorage / sessionStorage are JS-accessible and unsuitable for long-lived tokens; only short-TTL access tokens may live there, if at all. Fires exposure "Token exfiltration via XSS / JS-accessible storage".

Code grep: `localStorage.setItem('refresh`, `sessionStorage.setItem('refresh`, framework auth-store config (Auth0 SPA SDK `cacheLocation: 'localstorage'`) — these explicitly opt into the insecure pattern.

option_name: Refresh token rotation on every use
how_to_obtain: Authorization server config: confirm rotation is enabled (Auth0 application 'Refresh Token Rotation' toggle; Okta 'Rotate token after every use'; Keycloak realm 'Revoke Refresh Token' enabled; Cognito client 'EnableTokenRevocation').
RFC 9700 §2.2.2 'Refresh Token Protection' + OWASP OAuth2 Cheat Sheet — 'Refresh Token Rotation': single-use rotation is BCP for public clients.

Live probe: perform a refresh exchange against /token (`curl -X POST .../token -d 'grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<rt>'`); record the new refresh_token returned; immediately replay the ORIGINAL rt — rotation-on-use requires it to be rejected. Replay-acceptance fires exposure "Refresh-token replay with no rotation or reuse detection".
If the same rt remains usable across multiple refreshes, rotation is disabled; if the new rt arrives but the old one is still accepted, that is the worst-of-both case (rotation without invalidation).

option_name: Verifier vulnerable to RS256→HS256 key-confusion / kid injection
how_to_obtain: Code review: verifier must NOT branch on the token-supplied alg to choose the verification routine — it must pin the algorithm AND pin the key type for that alg. RFC 8725 §3.1 and §2.1 are the authoritative anchors.

Library API check: node-jsonwebtoken `algorithms: ['RS256']` (mandatory — absence allows HS256 selection against the RSA key); jjwt `Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(rsaPublicKey).build()` (pre-0.10 versions tolerate HS256 against the same key); PyJWT modern versions reject this, older do not.

Live probe (canonical exploit): take a valid RS256 token, change header to `{"alg":"HS256"}`, sign with the issuer's PEM public key as the HMAC secret (jwt_tool / scripted), present it — a 200 proves rs256_to_hs256_confusion_possible=true and fires exposure "JWT signature algorithm confusion".

kid header injection: inspect how the verifier resolves `kid` — it must look up against a trusted JWKS set, never a path/SQL value influenced by the kid string. Path-traversal-style kid values (`../../dev/null`) reaching the filesystem indicate the related kid-injection vulnerability (RFC 8725 §3.11).

option_name: SameSite attribute present on session cookie
how_to_obtain: Capture Set-Cookie: `curl -i .../login | grep -i '^set-cookie:'` and check each session cookie line for `SameSite=` (any value).

Browser DevTools Application → Cookies: the SameSite column shows the policy. Empty / 'Unspecified' (which Chrome currently treats as Lax-by-default) is reported as missing by this attestation — the attribute string must be present.

RFC 6265bis §4.1.2.7 + OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — 'SameSite Attribute': missing SameSite leaves CSRF auto-attachment to legacy browser defaults (Safari does not enforce Lax-by-default) and downgrades CSRF posture. Missing attribute fires exposure "Session fixation and cross-site request forgery on cookie-borne sessions".

Cross-browser test: open an attacker-controlled origin and trigger a state-changing POST to the app — if the session cookie attaches and the request succeeds, the SameSite control is effectively absent.
Capture Set-Cookie and read the value: `curl -i .../login | grep -i samesite=` returns `SameSite=Strict|Lax|None`. None requires `Secure` to be honoured by modern browsers (RFC 6265bis §5.5).

OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — 'SameSite Attribute': 'Strict' / 'Lax' protect state-changing endpoints from CSRF; 'None' opts back in to cross-site attachment. Rule fires when value equals 'None' — exposure "Session fixation and cross-site request forgery on cookie-borne sessions".
If the value is 'None', require justification (third-party embeds, federated logout) and a complementary CSRF token / Origin-header check on every state-changing endpoint.
Audit pattern: a session cookie with `SameSite=None` that is also missing `Secure` is rejected by modern Chrome — verify both attributes co-occur.

option_name: Tokens redacted from logs, traces, and error reports
how_to_obtain: Logging pipeline review: confirm a redaction filter for `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `id_token`, `Bearer ` (and JSON-body equivalents) on application logs, access logs, and OpenTelemetry span attributes. CWE-532 + OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet name these patterns.

OpenTelemetry / APM config: Sentry `beforeSend` scrubs `Authorization` headers; Datadog `processing_rules` strips token-shaped strings; OTel SDK `SpanProcessor` filters span attributes — verify by code/config grep.

Live test: send a request with a probe-value bearer token (`Authorization: Bearer DEADBEEF-PROBE-<uuid>`); then grep all log/telemetry sinks (application logs, nginx access logs, CDN logs, Sentry events, Datadog traces) for `DEADBEEF-PROBE-`. Any hit proves secrets_masked_in_logs=false and fires exposure "Token leakage via URL, Referer, or telemetry sinks".
MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001 'Credentials in Files' is the threat model — the log store is the file in question.

Authorization-server feature check — DPoP: issuer accepts `DPoP` request header on /token and binds the access token to the proof JWT's `cnf.jkt` thumbprint (RFC 9449 §6); mTLS: issuer accepts client-cert authentication and emits `cnf.x5t#S256` binding (RFC 8705 §3).
Inspect an issued access token: decode the JWT and look for a `cnf` (confirmation) claim — `cnf.jkt` indicates DPoP binding, `cnf.x5t#S256` indicates mTLS binding. Absence of `cnf` means pure bearer.

Resource-server check: confirm the API validates the DPoP proof on every request (header `DPoP: <proof-jwt>` with matching htm/htu/jti/ath claims per RFC 9449 §4.3) or terminates client TLS itself and matches the cert thumbprint. RFC 9700 §2.2 is the BCP.

Live replay test: capture a valid Authorization header and replay it from a different host without the corresponding DPoP proof / client cert — sender-constrained deployments return 401 'invalid_dpop_proof' / TLS handshake failure; pure bearers return 200, firing exposure "Bearer token theft and replay without sender constraint".

Endpoint discovery: query the authorization server's OIDC discovery document (`GET /.well-known/openid-configuration`) and confirm both `revocation_endpoint` (RFC 7009) and `introspection_endpoint` (RFC 7662) are advertised and reachable.

Live revocation test: revoke a token via `curl -X POST <revocation_endpoint> -d 'token=<rt>&token_type_hint=refresh_token' -u <client>`; then attempt to use it. RFC 7009 requires immediate invalidation; a 200 on subsequent use proves revocation is non-functional — fires both "Refresh-token replay with no rotation or reuse detection" and "Excessive token lifetime with no revocation channel".

Refresh-token reuse-detection probe (Auth0 / Okta family-invalidation guidance): refresh once (rt1 → rt2 + at2), then present rt1 again. The server MUST revoke the entire token family on detected reuse — verify that rt2 is also invalidated after the rt1 replay attempt.
Store check: for JWT-based deployments confirm a deny-list / token-id (jti) blocklist is consulted on every verification — otherwise self-contained JWTs cannot be pulled back.

Session-store / authorization-server config: locate the absolute-lifetime parameter (Keycloak realm 'SSO Session Max'; Auth0 tenant 'Absolute Lifetime'; Spring Session `maximumSessions` / `maxLifetime`; express-session does NOT support absolute by default — must be enforced in app code).
OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — 'Session Expiration' section: recommends idle + absolute timers; absolute typically 4–12 h or one working day regardless of activity.

Live test: authenticate, then continuously refresh / use the session past the documented absolute limit (script a request every 5 min beyond the cap); a session that survives indefinitely proves session_absolute_timeout_enforced=false and fires exposure "Excessive token lifetime with no revocation channel".

Cross-check refresh-chain extensibility: if refresh tokens reissue access tokens without consulting an absolute cap on the underlying session, the absolute timeout is bypassable through the refresh path.

option_name: Session id regenerated on authentication / privilege change
how_to_obtain: Live test: visit the site unauthenticated, record the pre-login session cookie value; submit valid credentials; record the post-login session cookie. Per OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — 'Renew the Session ID After Any Privilege Level Change' — they MUST differ. Identical values prove session_id_regenerated_on_auth=false (CWE-384 Session Fixation), firing exposure "Session fixation and cross-site request forgery on cookie-borne sessions".

Code grep for explicit regeneration: PHP `session_regenerate_id(true)`; Django `request.session.cycle_key()`; Spring Security `SessionFixationProtectionStrategy` / `migrateSession`; Express `req.session.regenerate(cb)`.
Repeat for every privilege transition: MFA step-up, password change, role escalation, account link — each MUST mint a fresh id per OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet — 'Re-Authentication'.
Confirm the server REJECTS server-unminted ids (strict, not permissive, session management) — try presenting a freshly-generated random session cookie; the server must not adopt it.

option_name: Signature algorithm pinned server-side (header alg ignored)
how_to_obtain: Library API check (the canonical control): verifier called with an explicit algorithms allow-list — node-jsonwebtoken `jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['RS256'] })`; PyJWT `jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256'])`; jjwt 0.11+ `Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(key).build()` (pins to the algorithm family of the supplied key); jose-jwt `JWT.Decode(token, key, JwsAlgorithm.RS256)`.
RFC 8725 §3.1 'Use Appropriate Algorithms' + §2.1 'Perform Algorithm Verification' — the verifier MUST NOT trust the token-supplied alg to choose the verification routine.

Live probe: take a valid token, rewrite the header alg to a different family (RS256 → HS256, or RS256 → none) without changing the signature segment; the verifier MUST reject. Acceptance proves pinning is absent and fires exposure "JWT signature algorithm confusion".
Configuration review: any verifier API that takes 'algorithm' as input from the token (some legacy wrappers) rather than from configuration is unsafe — call it out by name.

option_name: HMAC signing key generated by CSPRNG
how_to_obtain: Operator interview / runbook review: confirm key-generation used a CSPRNG — `openssl rand -base64 64`, `/dev/urandom`, `python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(64))'`, AWS KMS `GenerateRandom`, Vault `transit/random` — NOT a human-chosen string, passphrase without strong KDF, or `Math.random()`-class RNG.
RFC 8725 §3.5 'Use Appropriate Key Length' + RFC 4086 'Randomness Requirements for Security': cryptographic keys MUST be generated by a CSPRNG.

Audit the key in the secret store for tell-tale weakness: words, repeated patterns, ASCII-only short strings, common defaults ('secret', 'changeme', the project name). Any of these refute CSPRNG provenance regardless of stated procedure and fire exposure "Weak HMAC secret brute-force".

If the key was derived from a passphrase, verify a strong KDF was applied (Argon2id with documented parameters, PBKDF2 with ≥600k iterations per OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet) — otherwise the effective entropy is the passphrase's, not the output's.

option_name: HMAC signing key has high entropy (resists brute-force)
how_to_obtain: Measure key length in bytes from the secret store: ≥ 32 bytes (256 bits) for HS256 per RFC 7518 §3.2; ≥ 48 bytes for HS384; ≥ 64 bytes for HS512. Anything shorter than the hash output is the explicit RFC 7518 violation.

Offline crack attempt as falsification: `hashcat -m 16500 captured.jwt rockyou.txt -O` and `hashcat -m 16500 captured.jwt -a 3 ?a?a?a?a?a?a?a?a` (mask 8-char brute-force). A hit within hours proves signing_key_high_entropy=false and fires exposure "Weak HMAC secret brute-force".

RFC 8725 §3.5 + OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet — 'Symmetric Key Confidentiality and Strength': mandates long, random, never-reused symmetric secrets; prefers asymmetric (RS256/ES256/EdDSA) so this question becomes moot for verifiers.
Check default-value provenance: if the secret originated from the framework's example config or a tutorial copy-paste, treat entropy as zero regardless of measured length.

Browser DevTools — Application → Local Storage and Session Storage: enumerate entries; any access_token / id_token / refresh_token / `Bearer`-shaped value is JS-accessible storage. Application → Cookies: any auth cookie WITHOUT HttpOnly is equivalently JS-accessible.

Browser console: `Object.keys(localStorage)` and `Object.keys(sessionStorage)` from the authenticated page; `document.cookie` lists non-HttpOnly cookies. Any token-shaped value confirms stored_in_js_accessible_storage=true and fires exposure "Token exfiltration via XSS / JS-accessible storage".

OWASP JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet — 'Token Storage on Client Side' + RFC 9700 §4.13: localStorage / sessionStorage are reachable by injected script and unsuitable; HttpOnly cookies or non-persistent in-memory only is the safe pattern.

Code grep: `localStorage.setItem('token`, `localStorage.setItem('access`, framework auth library config (Auth0 SPA SDK `cacheLocation: 'localstorage'`, MSAL `cacheLocation: 'localStorage'`) — all opt into the insecure pattern explicitly.

HSTS check: `curl -sI https://app.example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security` — `max-age` should be ≥ 31536000 with `includeSubDomains` (and ideally `preload`). Per OWASP Secure Headers Project this prevents protocol downgrade.

Cleartext probe: `curl -v http://app.example.com/api/me -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'` — the server MUST 301/308 to https BEFORE any token-bearing endpoint accepts the request, AND the cookie/header must not be acknowledged on the plaintext leg. Failure fires exposure "Token leakage via URL, Referer, or telemetry sinks".

Issuer + revocation endpoints: `curl -v http://idp.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` — the discovery doc, /token, /revocation, /introspection MUST all be https-only on every leg of the token lifecycle (RFC 9700 §3.1).

Network capture in a staging environment: tcpdump / Wireshark on the egress interface during a login + API call; observe no plaintext token bytes. Mixed-mode (HTTPS with an HTTP redirect chain) counts as cleartext for this attestation.

option_name: Token appears in URL path / query / fragment
how_to_obtain: Inspect HTTP request shapes: tokens MUST live in `Authorization: Bearer` header or `Cookie:` header — NEVER in `?access_token=`, path segments, or `#access_token=` fragments. RFC 9700 §4.3.2 'Authorization Code in Browser History' + CWE-598 are the authorities.

Web-server / CDN access logs: `grep -E 'access_token=|token=|jwt=|sid=' /var/log/nginx/access.log` (and CloudFront / Cloudflare / Fastly logs) — any hit confirms tokens hit URLs and were logged. The hit itself is evidence of leakage to log sinks and fires exposure "Token leakage via URL, Referer, or telemetry sinks".

Browser history + Referer test: navigate from an authenticated page to a third-party origin (analytics pixel, embedded widget). Inspect outbound requests' `Referer` header in DevTools — token bytes in Referer prove URL-borne leakage to third parties. Mitigate with `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` or `strict-origin`.

Code grep: `window.location.href.includes('token=')`, route handlers reading `req.query.access_token`, OAuth implicit-flow callback handlers reading `window.location.hash` — flag any of these as URL-borne token paths (RFC 9700 deprecates implicit flow precisely because of this).
